New in this release · Rel 2.7a · 2 October 2026
Riding together starts with a rideRiding together starts with a ride. GroupTrack's community begins with the ride package — a route, starting at its defined trailhead, on a set date and time, with the maps it needs and its radio configuration. Send it to friends and riders who want to ride with you.One click, and everyone has the same preparation: the trailhead marked on their map, the route outlined to follow, the required maps downloaded along it. At the trailhead, check-in applies the ride's radio configuration for them. The fastest way to create one is a map touch: tap a route or a track on the Ride Planning Map, then CREATE RIDE — Manual: Map touches, the fastest way to Create a Ride.No more night before the ride spent downloading an area and hoping the trail goes where you think it does. No one asks where to meet, and no one waits at the trailhead while someone else catches up. Everyone's time goes to riding.

Earlier releases
DOCUMENT ID: RELNOTES-2026-08-29-B
Plan a ride
This release is about one thing: the route planner is finished. Tell it where you are
starting, how far you want to go and how fast you ride, and it brings back up to six routes for you
to compare.
How it works now
The planner asks one thing at a time. An overview explains what you will get. A second screen
sets your distance and pace, and shows the ride duration as you move the sliders — set the mileage
until the hours match the day you have.
After that each step puts a short prompt at the bottom of the screen and leaves the map clear
to work on. Pick where you will park. Drop pins on places the ride should reach, if you have any
in mind. Say whether you are looping back or finishing somewhere else. Then read back what is
about to be built, and press Continue to Compare.
Comparing the six
The routes are drawn on the map, each in its own colour, next to a table showing what each one
covers. Tap a route's name to hide or unhide its line, so you can see one at a time. Tick
the ones you want and press Save Selected / Delete Unselected — the ones you do not tick
are removed.
Build the same rides again
Every route the planner builds records the settings that produced it. Open a saved route and
press Build Routes From Recipe: it reads those settings back, shows you a summary, and
rebuilds. This is how you get back the alternatives you did not keep the first time.
The button only appears on routes the planner built — a route drawn by hand or imported from
another app has no settings to rebuild from.
Sharing a route
A shared route now carries its description with it. Export one and the summary the
planner wrote travels in the file, along with the settings that built it — so whoever you send it
to can build their own six routes from your parameters. Routes imported from Gaia or onX bring
their descriptions in the same way.
Fixes worth knowing about
Searching the same area twice. If you ran a search, then ran another in the same area
without closing the app, the second set could be worse than the first — points you asked the ride
to cover were more likely to be left out. Fixed.
Adding a trailhead now selects it. Previously you had to create one and then tap it
again.
The trailhead step opens with search ready, and a blue circle shows which trails are
close enough to start a route. Move the map until the trail you want is inside it.
Search tip: follow an area name with its two-character state. The same name exists in
many states and landing in the wrong one is not obvious — the map moves, trails draw, and
everything looks right.
What is coming next
Better trail data. The trails on your device today are selected by shape alone, which
means some paved neighbourhood roads come in as trails and some dirt roads you ride do not come in
at all. The next release fixes that, and adds trail types you can filter — so you can turn hiking
trails off, or see at a glance which parts of a route are on ground built for vehicles.
⚠ One thing to expect when it arrives: your saved routes are safe and will still draw
and navigate. But rebuilding one from its recipe may return different alternatives than it does
today, because the ground the planner can see will have changed. That is the improvement working,
not a fault.
— carried forward —
DOCUMENT ID: RELNOTES-2026-08-29
2026-09-17 — importing a state outside Utah now finishes
Imports outside Utah stopped at the last step
If you imported the trails for a state other than Utah and GroupTrack closed near the end, this
was the reason. The last step checks which trails cross private land, using a land-ownership map —
and that map only covers Utah. GroupTrack was downloading it and working through all of it for every
state, including ones it could never apply to. On most tablets that ran out of memory right at the end.
It now only does that work for Utah, where the data applies, and it reads Utah's map far more
efficiently. If an import of your state stopped before, run it again.
⚠ If the import screen won't start after an import was interrupted — you pick your state and
nothing happens — close GroupTrack completely (swipe it away from your recent apps, or use Force stop in
Android's app settings) and open it again. A fix for that is coming.
Maps are ticked for you when you import
The option to download the maps along with the trails is now switched on when the import screen
opens, and easier to read. Untick it if you only want the trails.
2026-09-15 — your location, and a map that stays where you put it
Tablets and phones without their own GPS
If your device has no GPS chip, GroupTrack could not find you at all. Your cart showed
its name but no position, and the map opened on a view of the whole country instead of where you
were. The app now also asks your network connection for a location, which is how a device without
GPS knows where it is.
And it now tells you when that is what is happening. A network location works at home
and in the car park. It does not work on the trail, because there is no network out there. If
GroupTrack is locating you that way you will see a message saying so once, with the option not to
be told again.
⚠ A device with no GPS of its own needs a mesh radio to work off-grid. The radio carries
its own GPS, so it answers both problems at once — it knows where you are and it shares that with
your group. We recommend the Seeed SenseCAP Card Tracker T1000-E.
If the app cannot find you by any means at all, it now says that too, rather than quietly
showing you an empty map.
My Cart stopped fighting the zoom
On topo maps the view jumped in and out every couple of seconds. My Cart was asking to
zoom closer than the map has detail for, the map pushed back, and round it went. My Cart now asks
for the closest zoom the map you are on actually has — so it settles and stays.
You can still pinch in past that. The picture is enlarged rather than sharper, which is the
point: your tracks and waypoints stay crisp so you can place one precisely.
Searching for a place now leaves you there
Search an area from the ride map and it used to snap back to your own cart a second or two
later. Following your cart is now switched off when a search moves the map, exactly as it is
when you drag the map with your finger. Look around as long as you like; tap MY CART when you
want to come back, and following starts again.
Searching for a track, route, trail or waypoint by name is unchanged — that opens its details
without moving the map, so you stay followed.
Smaller topo downloads
Topo maps were downloading two zoom levels the app never draws. Those levels are roughly
four times the size of the one below, each, so a topo download was several times larger than it
needed to be with nothing to show for it. They are no longer fetched. Satellite is unchanged —
it has real detail at every level it offers.
⚠ The estimate shown before a download still counts those levels, so it will read higher than
what actually arrives.
Maps failing to appear
In some situations the app could lose track of which map sources it had and fall back to
a built-in list that did not include the one you had chosen — which showed up as a blank map on
every source. It now reads your actual map settings instead of guessing.
2026-09-13 — start here
Two paths below. Open the one that applies to you.
First time installing GroupTrack
1 &middot; Grant location
GroupTrack needs your location all the time — it is how the app keeps
your position on the map and how the convoy sees where you are while you ride.
Follow the prompts.
2 &middot; Choose your home state
Let it download the trails. It takes around 25 minutes and it only happens
once. After that the trails work with no signal, which is most of where you
ride.
3 &middot; Import your track history
Do this before you start building routes. Every track you bring in adds
its trails to the trail database — so the more of your riding history you
import, the more complete your map becomes.
Put your GPX files in Downloads on your Android: save them from an email
attachment, or download them straight from your navigation app.
Then tap Import Trails on the Map Features screen from the
planning map. You will be asked to pick the files.
To select several files at once, press and hold the first file, then tap the others.
4 &middot; Ride
When the app has your location, you are ready to go.
Updating from an earlier version
Your data moves once, on the first launch
GroupTrack used to keep your trails, tracks, routes and maps in your phone's
Documents folder. It now keeps them in its own storage instead.
The first time you open this version it asks you to choose a folder. Choose
Documents and allow access. Everything moves across on its own.
Your data takes a couple of minutes. Your maps are handled separately and take
longer — a large map store can run up to 15 minutes. Leave the screen open while
it works.
If there is not enough room for your maps
Maps need space to move. If there is not enough, GroupTrack tells you, and
those maps are deleted — you will need to download them again when you
have room. Everything else still moves across.
Importing tracks has changed
GroupTrack no longer searches your Downloads folder by itself. Tap
Import Trails on the Map Features screen and you will be asked to
pick the files you want.
To select several files at once, press and hold the first file, then tap the others.
And this is worth doing with your whole track history. Every track you
import adds its trails to the trail database, so bringing in years of old tracks
fills out your map in a way nothing else does. Put the GPX files in
Downloads first — from an email attachment or straight from your
navigation app.
Why the change
Google restricts which apps may keep files in shared folders like Documents.
Rather than ask for an exception, GroupTrack now stores its own data in its own
place — which is what the rules are for.
One thing worth knowing: data kept this way is removed if you uninstall the
app. Use the share options to keep a copy of any route or track you would not
want to lose.
2026-09-12 — where GroupTrack keeps your data
A one-time move, and one tap from you
GroupTrack used to keep your trails, tracks, routes and downloaded maps
in your phone's Documents folder. It now keeps them in its own storage
instead.
The first time you open this version it will ask you to select your
Documents folder. Tap it, and everything moves across on its own — trails,
tracks, routes, waypoints, your saved colours, and your downloaded maps if
there is room for them. If you are new to GroupTrack there is nothing to
move and it simply carries on.
Your maps are the slow part. Everything else takes under a minute; a large
map store can take several. Leave the screen open while it works.
Why the change
Google restricts which apps may keep files in shared folders like
Documents. Rather than ask for an exception, GroupTrack now stores its own
data in its own place — which is what the rules are for.
One thing worth knowing: data kept this way is removed if you uninstall
the app. Use the share options to keep a copy of any route or track you would
not want to lose.
2026-09-11 — your colours stay yours
The map keys now work the way you would expect
Set a trail type to the colour, line pattern or thickness you want, and
the map draws it that way from the moment it opens — on the ride map and
the planning map both. Previously your choices only reached the map after you
opened the key panel and changed something, so a setting could appear to
revert every time you restarted the app. It was never lost; the map simply
was not being told.
Routes draw solid
Saved routes were drawn with a long dashed line that was almost
indistinguishable from a solid one, even zoomed right in. They are solid now,
like every other line you can ride, and the key panel matches. Your recorded
tracks are still dashed — that pattern is visible and it tells the two
apart.
2026-09-10 — the map answers when you tap it
Tapping things on the ride map
Tapping a trail, track or route on the ride map now opens its detail
panel. Tracks in particular were hard to hit — the line is thin and dashed,
and zoomed in there was very little to aim at. There is now a wider invisible
target along every track, so a tap near the line works. Nothing looks
different.
What the categories mean
The map key panel has a new CATEGORIES EXPLAINED button at the
foot, beside My tracks and My routes. It says in plain words what each trail
type is.
Two are worth knowing before you plan on them. Rider trails are
ground you have actually ridden, so a machine has been there — a stronger
claim than any survey. Forestry / access roads are open unless posted
otherwise, so look for a sign at the gate.
Map sources
If the app was opened while it was busy — during a state import, or the
first launch after an update — it could come up showing three map sources
instead of the full list, and ignore the ones you had chosen. Restarting was
the only cure. It now recovers on its own.
2026-09-08 — the ground you have ridden becomes trails
NEW Share a route and its narrative goes with it
Send a route to another rider and they get the whole thing — the summary, what
they will see along the way, the cautions, and the settings it was built from.
They can press BUILD FROM RECIPE and search again on their own device.
They may get different routes than you did, because the recipe is a set of
instructions rather than a copy of your answer — and their trail data is not
yours.
Opened in Gaia or onX the route still reads normally; those apps see the name,
description and points and ignore the rest.
NEW Remove a trail you added
Tap one of your own rider trails and there is now a DELETE button.
Surveyed trails do not have one.
Mostly useful when a recorder was left running on the drive to the trailhead —
highways are not in the trail data, so the whole drive comes in as new ground.
FIXED Tapping a route on the ride map
It opened a small bubble, or nothing at all. It now opens the full detail
panel, the same as the planning map.
Trails, tracks and routes also draw in proper order now — trails widest and
underneath, then tracks, then routes — so where all three share ground you can
see each of them and tap the one you meant.
⭐⭐ DO THIS FIRST — import your track history before you plan a route
If you skip this, the route planner will send you the long way around
ground you have already ridden. It cannot use a trail it does not have, and
published maps are missing a great deal of what riders actually use.
The order that gets you the best routes:
Load every state you ride in — including ones you only cross into. A
ride that leaves your loaded states has no trail data underneath it.
Import your recorded TRACKS — your saved rides from onX, Gaia or
anywhere else. ⚠ Tracks, not routes: a route is a plan, a track is where you
actually went, and only a track proves the ground is rideable.
Then build your routes.
Already built routes before importing? Rebuild them. They will come
back different, and that is the point — the planner can finally see the ground
you know.
NEW Your tracks fill in what the maps miss
Published trail data leaves a lot out. Roads and tracks that get ridden every
weekend are simply not in it, and until now that ground did not exist as far as
the app was concerned.
Now, where one of your recorded tracks crosses ground with no trail underneath
it, GroupTrack adds that stretch as a trail. It is unnamed, drawn in its own
colour, and behaves like any other trail — you can filter it, tap it, and the
route planner can use it.
Tested on one rider's collection: 88 tracks produced 1,872 new trails
covering about 2,400 miles of ground that no published source had.
NEW Import your old tracks — all of them
Export every track you have from onX, Gaia or wherever else you have
kept them, and import the lot. ⚠ Tracks, not routes. A route is a plan
somebody drew; a track is where a rider actually went. Only a track is evidence
that the ground goes through.
This is the single most useful thing you can do before using the route
planner. Every track you bring in is ground the planner can then route you
over. Without them it is working from published trails alone — and it will route
you around trails you have ridden a dozen times, with no way for you to know why.
Load your states first. A ride crossing into a state you have not
imported has no trails underneath it, so the whole stretch is treated as new
ground even where trails already exist. After that the order does not matter —
each track is checked as it arrives.
NEW Add trails from tracks, on demand
There is a new ADD TRAILS FROM TRACKS button under RESYNC TRACKS on the
import panel. It reads every track you already have and adds whatever ground is
missing. Safe to press more than once — a second run finds nothing, because the
first one already covered it.
CHANGED The trail import says what it is doing
The long stretch in the middle of a state import used to sit on
Processing for ten minutes without moving. It now shows what is being
worked on and how far through it is.
The import also has a new step of its own — Trails from tracks — which
runs after your trail data has loaded and reports how many it added.
⚠ Worth knowing
Routes you built before will come back different. With more network to
work with, the planner finds rides it could not find before. That is the
improvement working.
A trail from your ride is honest, not authoritative. It says you rode
that ground — not that it is maintained, public, or open to anyone else. Check
ownership and access the way you would anywhere else.
2026-09-04 — hide the radio panels if you do not use them
The Meshtastic column folds away
The list down the left side of the app belongs to Meshtastic, the radio
software GroupTrack is built on. If you ride with a tablet alone, none of it is
for you.
Hide Mesh at the bottom of that column folds the whole thing away.
A Mesh button then appears with Map Features and Help on the right of
either map — tap it to bring the column back. GroupTrack remembers which you
chose.
The radio menu says what it is for
The GroupTrack tab is now GroupTrack Mesh Radio Setup, and the menu
behind it is titled the same. Everything in it is radio work and nothing else,
so it is clear at a glance whether it concerns you.
Its five entries now name what they do — creating a ride's radio
configuration, sending it, importing one, applying it to your radio, and
restoring a saved one. The Map Settings section has gone; everything live in it
is reachable elsewhere.
Saved routes are named more sensibly
Saving several routes from one search used to give them all the same name.
They now carry a number — Broken Ridge Route 1, 2, and so on.
The mileage and point count have come out of the name, since tapping a route
shows the distance and riding time anyway.
Routes you saved before this keep the names they have.
2026-09-03 — tap a route and see what the ride is
One tap from the map to the ride
Tap any route you have saved and it opens with the description of the ride —
how far, how long, what you will see, and the stops in the order you reach them.
Previously that was three screens away.
The long lists start folded so the distance, the riding time and the warnings
are what you see first. Tap a heading to open one.
Two things you can do from there without leaving: Download maps for the
route's area, and Route details for the full record.
Routes built before the app started writing descriptions open the details
panel as they always did.
The import tells you the truth about itself
Classifying the trails — working out which are motorized and which sit on
private ground — is now listed as its own step when a state loads, with its own
count. Before, it ran silently at the end and a failure could look like a
finished import.
And the summary at the end of an import now waits for you. If you put the
phone down while a state loads and come back later, it is still there.
Smaller things
Only one state import runs at a time, and cancelling one actually
stops it.
Riding time shows as a range in the comparison table, not just the
faster number.
Each trail in a comparison shows its surface beside the mileage.
Tapping a trail on the ride map opens its record, as it already did on
the planning map.
Search sits where the other buttons do on both maps.
Field names read as English — Roughness rather than smoothness, Land rather
than land_status.
⚠ This update reloads your trails
The first launch after installing clears the trail data and asks you to import
your state again — about twenty minutes for a large state. A red
SYSTEM HOUSEKEEPING message appears while it prepares, and Continue turns
on by itself when it is safe.
Your maps, tracks, routes and waypoints are not affected.
2026-09-02 — choose which trails you see, and pick your own colours
Choosing what shows moved to Map Features
Yesterday's Map Keys panel did two jobs. It now does one. Which trails appear is chosen from
Map Features › Trails › SELECT — the same place you have always chosen what shows for tracks,
waypoints and routes. Everything is in one place instead of trails being the exception.
That panel has the two groups, Motorized and Non-motorized, with a tick beside each type, and a
single Include private land option. Untick a type and it goes; tap a heading and the whole
group goes. And OFF on the Trails row still hides every trail in one tap when you want the map
clear.
Map Keys is now the key — and where you set the colours
It shows what each line means. Tap the name of any type and you can change its colour, its
pattern and how thick it draws. The panel shows the line as it is now beside the line as it would be,
so you can compare before you commit. Apply, and the map changes.
What you choose is yours and it stays. The colours the app ships with are simply a starting point.
The lines tell you what you can ride
Solid lines are motorized. Dotted lines are not. That is the first thing to read on the map,
and it does not depend on telling colours apart in bright sun.
The app now also ships knowing, for every trail, whether it sits on public or private ground and
whether it is a motorized route — worked out during the import from the state's land-ownership records
and from what each source published. That is what the filter acts on.
Tap a trail and see what is actually known about it
Trails used to show a small bubble with a name. They now open the same detail card that tracks and
routes do, showing everything the sources published and nothing they did not — the surface, who
manages it, any posted restrictions, and where the record came from.
Where a trail carries a roughness rating it is written plainly: "Severe — ATV or tractor"
rather than a code. It is only recorded on a minority of trails, but where it exists it is the one
thing that tells you whether a machine will get through.
Smaller things
Search now moves the map to what you pick. Choosing a result frames it — no second step.
Search has a close button. So do Map Features, the route toolbar and the comparison table.
Route+ has an X that closes it without discarding your work. Closing and discarding are
different things and now look different.
Help offers three documents — Quick Start, Release Notes and the Full Manual — and a Cancel
if you opened it by accident.
The comparison table can be dragged out of the way.
Route planning builds on the trails you have chosen to see. If you hide a type, the planner
stops using it. What is on the map is what gets routed.
⚠ This update reloads your trails
The first launch after installing clears the trail data and asks you to import your state again.
It takes about twenty minutes for a large state. This is necessary — the new information about land
ownership and trail type is worked out during the import, and it cannot be added to data that is
already loaded.
Your maps, tracks, routes and waypoints are not affected. Only trail data reloads.
⚠ Worth knowing on first run
The app starts by showing motorized trails on public land. Hiking, biking and equestrian
trails are hidden, and so is private ground. That is deliberate for an off-road app — but if you are
looking for a trail you know exists and cannot see it, that is why. Map Features › Trails › SELECT
turns them back on.
2026-09-01 — the map key becomes a filter, and the town roads can be turned off
A new Map Keys panel, on both maps
The key that explains the colours has become something you can use. It is on the convoy map now
as well as the planning map — the convoy map never had one before. On the convoy map it opens from
the new Map Keys button, between Map Features and Help.
Inside it, the trail types are grouped into Motorized and Non-motorized, side by
side. Every type starts switched on. Unchecking a row hides that type; tapping a column heading
hides the whole group.
Public and private land
The panel has one filter at the top: Both, Public, or Private. Choosing
Public hides everything that sits on private land — which, near a town, is most of the street grid.
If you have been zooming past a mess of residential streets to find the trail you actually want,
this is the switch for that.
Choosing Private does the opposite, which is useful when a private road is how you get from one
piece of public ground to the next.
Whatever you choose is remembered and applied the next time you open the map.
The colours changed
Anything you can ride is now a shade of blue, and the shade tells you how confident the app is:
Brightest blue — an OHV route, stated as such by the people who manage it
Blue — a track
Darker blue — a forestry or access road
Faint dashed blue — the app knows a line is there and nothing more
Green, yellow, purple and brown are walking, biking and horse trails. Deep pink is a residential
road on private land. A red dashed line means the trail is recorded as unofficial or uncertain —
worth knowing before you commit to it.
More detail behind each trail
The app now keeps a great deal more of what each source publishes — surface, trail class, which
system it belongs to, which agency manages it, and any posted restrictions. None of it is on screen
yet; it is being kept so it can be shown, and used for route building, in a coming release.
Known issue
Some trails that are in the app's records are not drawing on the map. We have confirmed the trail
data itself is correct and are tracing where they are being lost on the way to the screen. If you
know a trail exists and cannot see it, that is this problem and not your data.
2026-08-31 — better trail information
Trail data now carries what the source published about each piece of ground —
its type, who manages it, and whether it sits on public or private land. It is
what makes the trail filter and the land setting work.
Much of this is groundwork you will not see directly. What you will notice is
that tapping a trail tells you more than it used to.
2026-08-30 — the app stops freezing when trail data is cleared
Clearing trail data could lock the app up on startup. It no longer does.
The rest of this release was work on how trail data is brought in and sorted —
nothing visible, but it is what the classification and filtering are built on.
2026-08-29 — build the same rides again, and a fix worth knowing about
Build six more routes from a route you kept
Open any route the planner built for you and you will find Build Routes From Recipe under
its overview. One press and it rebuilds from the same settings — the same starting point, the same
distance, the same points you asked it to cover — and shows you what it is about to do before it
runs.
The button only appears on routes the planner built. A route you drew by hand, or imported from
somewhere else, has no settings to rebuild from.
A fix: searching the same area twice
If you searched an area, then searched it again without closing the app, the second set of
rides could be worse than the first. Points you asked the ride to cover were more likely to be
left out. This is fixed — the second search now starts from the same clean slate as the first.
Also in this release
The trailhead step opens with search ready, and a blue circle shows which trails are
close enough to start a route. Move the map until the trail you want is inside it.
Adding a trailhead now selects it. Previously you had to create one and then tap it
again.
Search tip: follow an area name with its two-character state — the same name often
exists in several states, and landing in the wrong one is not obvious.
The route toolbar no longer appears over the planning screens.
Route details shows Overview rather than Narrative.

DOCUMENT ID: RELNOTES-2026-08-28
2026-08-28 — the route planner walks you through it
Planning a route is now a set of screens that ask one thing at a time. Instead of a
checklist you read all at once, each step tells you what it needs, you do it on the map, and the
next step appears.
What you will see
An overview first, explaining what you will get and what happens to the routes you do
not keep. Tick the box and you will not see it again.
Distance and pace on their own screen, with the ride duration updating as you move the
sliders. Set the mileage until the hours match the day you have.
One prompt per step after that, sitting at the bottom of the screen so the map and the
search box stay clear.
A pin the planner cannot reach is removed, and it tells you why rather than quietly
building a route that misses it.
Save Selected / Delete Unselected spells out both halves, and the comparison now says
that tapping a route name hides its line.
Planning stays in portrait throughout, and the map layers are cleared before the comparison so
the routes are readable.
— carried forward from 2026-08-27 —
DOCUMENT ID: RELNOTES-2026-08-27
2026-08-27 — comparing the routes the app suggests
When the planner finds you rides, you can now see them side by side. Ask for routes and
the app draws every one it found, each in its own colour, with a table underneath that lines them
up against each other.
What you will see
Every route on the map at once, in its own colour.
A table where the rows are places and trails and each column is one route. A green
check means that route reaches that feature; a number means how many miles of that trail it
uses.
The most-used trails at the top. The trails near the top are what these rides are made
of; the ones lower down are what makes them different. Two routes with big numbers on the same few
trails are variations on the same ride.
Tap a route's name to take its line off the map so you can see the others. Tap again to
bring it back.
Tick the ones you want to keep, type a name for the area, and they are saved —
Panguitch Mi. 79 Pts. 7. The ones you did not tick are discarded.
While you are comparing
Trails, tracks and waypoints are hidden so the routes are readable, and put back exactly as
you had them when you leave. The map does not switch to route-drawing mode, so tapping a route
to look at it will not add points to it.
Leaving without saving keeps everything — the routes are still there next time you tap Route+.
Only Save Selected finishes the job. If you tick nothing, the app asks first: all the routes
go, and you would have to start the search over.
Also fixed
The In-Progress list no longer opens empty — with nothing to continue, Route+ simply starts a
new route.
Renaming an in-progress route has been removed. The name you give a route when you save it is
the one that matters.
Saved routes follow the trail correctly even when part of the route is off the edge of the
screen.

DOCUMENT ID RELNOTES-2026-08-26-r2 &middot; issued 26 August 2026
GroupTrack Release Notes
V2.6h &middot; in development &middot; RELNOTES-2026-08-26
These notes ship inside the app, so they always describe the build you
are running.
Document revision RELNOTES-2.6h-r2 &middot; 26 August 2026
What changed in this release
Which document you want
QuickStart is for a new rider on a first install &mdash; getting the app on
the phone, permissions, radio pairing, and getting trails onto the map. It is a summary of how
things work right now, not a history. It opens by itself the first time you install.
These release notes are for riders who already have GroupTrack. They cover
what is new in this release and how to use it, and they open after an update. Earlier releases
are kept below under Release history.
The user manual is the walkthrough. Where something new needs more than a paragraph,
these notes point at the manual page for it.
Route planning is being rebuilt &mdash; not ready to use yet
What this means to you. Nothing in this build, and that is deliberate.
The part of GroupTrack that suggests rides was taken apart and rebuilt this week. It now works
properly on the bench &mdash; it will offer you several genuinely different rides from where
you park, rather than one &mdash; but the screens you would use it through are still being
finished.
How to use it. You cannot yet. It is listed here so you know it is
coming and that the quiet in this area is work, not neglect.
Manual: Planning a route &mdash; link pending anchors
Files other riders send you now import completely
What this means to you. When someone emails you a GPX file and you tap
it, everything in it comes across &mdash; the tracks, the waypoints and the routes. Before, only
the tracks arrived and the rest were dropped without saying so, which is why a file could look
like it imported nothing. If you learned to save files to Downloads first as a workaround, you
no longer need to.
How to use it. Tap the attachment in your email and choose GroupTrack.
Importing from Map Features &rarr; IMPORT TRACKS, WAYPOINTS &amp; ROUTES still works and
gives the same result.
Manual: Importing files &mdash; link pending anchors
Your trails stay put
What this means to you. If you loaded your state and found the trails
gone again a day or two later, that is fixed. It was a one-time cleanup that kept running every
time the app opened instead of once. You should not have to load a state twice.
How to use it. Nothing to do. If your trails are missing right now, import
your state one more time and it will stay.
Manual: Loading trails for your state &mdash; link pending anchors
Route planning &mdash; not ready yet
What this means to you. Nothing yet. Work is going on behind the scenes
to let GroupTrack suggest rides from your trail data, and to let you mark places a ride has to
reach. It is not finished and is not something to rely on in this build. It is listed here so
you know it is coming, not so you can try it.
Known issues as of 26 August 2026
KNOWN A state import can stop partway. Some sources
finish and the rest never start. Your trail count still looks reasonable, so nothing appears
wrong &mdash; but the largest source, Open Source Maps, is usually the one that did not
run, and it carries most of the trail network.
What it looks like: route building offers one route where you would
expect several, or comes back well short of the distance you asked for. The map still shows
plenty of trails, which is what makes it confusing.
What to do: run the state import again. Trails already on your device are skipped, so
only what is missing is fetched and nothing is duplicated.
KNOWN Route planning near a town suggests roads.
The trail data GroupTrack imports contains roads as well as trails, and it cannot yet tell them
apart. Planning from a staging point inside a town will offer you rides that follow streets.
What to do: plan from where the trails actually start &mdash; a
trailhead or a parking area out of town. Work to separate roads from trails in the imported
data is underway.
KNOWN An import record can be opened by the wrong import
routine. The record left behind by a run is picked up by an older code path than the one
that wrote it, so a run can be misread afterwards &mdash; and a stopped import may be reported
inaccurately. Being fixed by pointing the existing routine at the current one rather than
leaving two.
KNOWN Some trail sources report errors on every record in
some areas. Affected in some areas and not others; under investigation. The per-source
counts on the completion screen are what make it visible.
KNOWN A state may be listed for your area without having
trails in it. States are matched using a rectangle around each state and those rectangles
overlap. It costs download time; it does not affect your data.
KNOWN Re-importing the same state on the same day
replaces that day's earlier import record.
Release history
Earlier releases, newest first. Each one shows what changed at the time.
V2.6g &mdash; 23 August 2026 &mdash; Home State Import Pipeline
Release date: In development · Branch: feature/convoy-event-ride
Importing routes and waypoints from a GPX file
FIX GPX files containing routes or waypoints now import.
Previously only the tracks in a file were read — routes and waypoints were skipped without any
message, so a file that contained them appeared to import nothing.
This affects files shared between riders, and exports from other apps.
HOW TO IMPORT
Save the file to your Downloads folder first, then open Map Features on the Ride
Planning Map and choose IMPORT TRACKS, WAYPOINTS &amp; ROUTES.
Tapping a GPX attachment directly in your email will not import routes yet — it still
reads tracks only. Save it to Downloads and import it from Map Features instead. This is being
worked on.
Note: the file is removed from Downloads once it has been imported.
Trail sources
FIX US Geological Survey National Trails now imports. Every
record from this source was failing, in every state, and the source appeared simply to have no
data for your area. It was reading the wrong field names from the service. In New Hampshire it
now brings in 390 trails where it previously brought none.
Import Trails — by State or by Area (New)
NEW Import Trails now asks how you want to choose your ground.
One button on the Map Features panel, two ways in:
By State — pick any state from the list. Every available source for that state is
processed. Use this when you're planning a trip somewhere new.
By Area — draw a box on the map. GroupTrack works out which states your box reaches and
processes every source that covers it. Your box can cross state lines — a ride that runs from
Utah into Arizona brings in both.
Either way there is no source checklist. Every source that covers your ground runs, because that
is what lets one source fill in what another is missing.
Import Progress Detail
NEW Every import now records what happened to each record, not just
how many were added. Per source: how many were read, how many fell inside your state or area, how
many you already had, how many were added, and how many could not be processed.
The summary still shows one number — records added. The detail sits behind the source name if you
want it, and it is written into the import record on your device either way, so it can be looked up
later.
CHANGE Each import run now carries an identifier, so a run can be
identified exactly when something needs looking into.
Known Issues
Some sources report errors on every record in some areas. US Geological Survey
National Trails is fixed (see above). Other sources are still affected in some areas and not
others — under investigation. These sources previously reported zero records with no indication
anything had gone wrong; the new counts are what made it visible.
A state may be listed for your area without having trails in it. States are matched using
a rectangle around each state and those rectangles overlap, so a neighbouring state can be included
and then contribute nothing. It costs download time; it does not affect your data. A way to skip
those states is coming.
Re-importing the same state on the same day replaces that day's earlier import record.
Home State Setup (New)
NEW One-tap trail data setup on first launch. When GroupTrack detects no trail data, it offers to load your home state's trails automatically:
GPS auto-detection suggests your state (uses Android Geocoder for accuracy at state borders)
Searchable state picker with all 50 US states + DC + PR + USVI
California split into North (San Luis Obispo area and north) and South (Santa Barbara/Bakersfield area and south)
All available data sources processed automatically — US Forest Service, US Geological Survey, National Park Service, state agencies, and Open Source Maps (Geofabrik OSM)
Progress display: per-source step indicators (✅/►/○), download progress in MB, running elapsed clock
Blinking "Do not close GroupTrack" banner during processing
Completion summary with per-source record counts and grand total
New Hampshire verified: 42,338 OSM trails + 1,010 catalog trails imported in ~4 minutes
Geofabrik State Asset
NEW Shipped geofabrik_states.json — 54 entries with download URLs for every US state and territory. Supports the automatic Geofabrik GPKG download (302 redirect handling included). Refreshable via update_geofabrik_states.py.
Release-Assets Folder
NEW release-assets/ folder in the repo. Holds dated docs (manual, release notes, quickstart) and two Python scripts. One command (python release-assets/prepare_release_assets.py) refreshes Geofabrik URLs, copies newest dated docs to app assets, and verifies markers.
Source Name Improvements
CHANGE Plain-language source names throughout — no unexplained acronyms:
UGRC Utah Trails → Utah Trails and Pathways
BLM Ground Transportation → Bureau of Land Management Trails
USFS National Forest System Trails → US Forest Service Trails
USGS National Trails → US Geological Survey National Trails
NPS Public Trails → National Park Service Trails
USFS Motor Vehicle Use Maps → US Forest Service Motor Vehicle Use Maps
OSM Trails → Open Source Maps
Bug Fixes
FIX Geofabrik -latest- URL 302 redirect now followed automatically.
FIX GPS state detection at border areas (NH/MA) now uses Android Geocoder instead of bbox matching.
FIX OSM import ledger creation before pending bbox set (prevented silent import failure).
Resolved since the 20 August notes
Home State setup now runs on first launch — it no longer has to be found on the Map
Features panel.
Import Trails by Area is built — draw a box, and every source covering it is processed,
across state lines.
The completion screen shows the full picture — records read, records in your area,
duplicates, added, and anything that could not be processed.

GroupTrack 2.7c — in development
Not yet released · One Map: one map, every tool, a cleaner screen
2.7c replaces the ride map and the planning map with one map. While it is being finished it is switched on in Settings › Layout (One Map). Everything you could do on either map is on it, reached from a few buttons around the edge.
In development · Rel 2.7c
CHANGED Trail imports no longer rebuild your trails from tracksTrails from your tracks are made the moment a track is saved or imported, ridden ground counted as motorized and public. Map › Import map features › Create trails from tracks is there for tracks you had before this was automatic. 24 OctWhat it means for you: trail imports finish sooner, and your trails from tracks are always complete.
CHANGED Trail imports classify only what they addedAfter an import, only the new trails are given their type, use and public / private land — seconds instead of minutes. Assign Utah private property still reassigns every trail when you ask it to. 24 OctWhat it means for you: an import ends quickly, and nothing you already have is changed by it.
CHANGED Every screen in one lookOver the satellite map every panel is white with blue writing; over the topo map it is blue with white writing. GroupTrack 2.7b — internal testing
22 October 2026 · one week with internal testers before release
Most of 2.7b is under the hood. GroupTrack and the radio side now talk through one connection, and the ride map is drawn only from the messages your tablet actually receives, instead of a 5-second polling loop. You should see a steadier map and a quicker response; what you do on the trail is the same. The changes you will notice:
Group awareness, or this tablet only &mdash; ride without a radio and GroupTrack hides everything that needs one. 13 Oct
The lead's track &mdash; solid bright blue ahead of you, your own track dashed blue; behind you the lead's track gives way to yours. 20 Oct
When the lead goes quiet &mdash; his cart keeps moving at an estimate, and his real path is filled in when he is heard again. 20 Oct and below
The radio link &mdash; "Your radio isn't answering" tells you what to do; losing satellites no longer disconnects the radio. 18 Oct
Roles &mdash; strict: no Leader, no lead; two riders on one role both go back to Rider. 15 Oct
Smaller things &mdash; recording pauses after 25 idle minutes instead of 10, a GPS light above REC, arrows on your route, Medium Fast or Long Fast in the GPS panel, Ride statistics in Settings, NODES instead of the Meshtastic side menu, and fixes to a white map at start and to a recording that paused itself.

GroupTrack never guesses which way he turned. If he was not steadily on any track or trail, the estimate stays where he was last heard. GroupTrack 2.7a — the Community release
Group communication and ride sharing · 30 September 2026
GroupTrack is complete as installed, and 2.7a adds your community. It is two products in one: a complete personal navigation product that lets you share rides and maps with other GroupTrack users, and a true situational awareness product for your group on the trail.
On your own — the whole job
Trails and maps on your device, working with no signal; a planner that builds routes for you to compare; waypoints, map downloads and your own track recordings. Manual: The Ride Planning Map
New: ★ Create a RideOne ride holds the route, the trailhead, the date and time, the maps to download and the mesh radio configuration. Send it in one click; your friends open it in one click — and ride anywhere off grid in total confidence. Manual: ★ Create a Ride
Your identity
Your rider profile — callsign and email — is who you are in GroupTrack. It is private: it stays on your tablet, nothing is sent to GroupTrack, and it goes only to the riders you ride with. Manual: Your rider profile
Add a radio to experience full group awareness while riding
Add a Meshtastic radio — any Meshtastic radio, not only the T1000-E — and you see your group on the map with no cell service. GroupTrack sets the radio up for you. Manual: Group Awareness
A private network for organizers and clubs — your rides use your own radio network; riders who have ridden with you are already on it next time, and nobody outside the ride hears it.
One standard language — radios report in TAK, the team-awareness format: your position with your callsign, even with the tablet in your pocket.
Roles and presence — Leader, Middle and Tail gunner are broadcast to every member; riders check in to claim a role and announce that they are there.
The ride carries the radio settings — checking in at the trailhead sets your radio up for the ride's network by itself.
So a ride goes like this
Tap the Ride invite. GroupTrack creates the route, its trailhead and the ride's description, stores the ride's radio settings, and imports the maps along the route.
With a radio, check in at the trailhead. Your radio is set up for the ride, and your role is announced.
REC. You are riding — with your group on the map if you carry a radio.
For the organizer it is one step: build the ride and send it.
2.7a update · 17 October 2026 (release m)Offline maps now open with no signal. Before this update, downloaded maps only showed if GroupTrack was started with an internet connection; started with no signal, the map stayed blank. The map library is now inside the app, so the map opens anywhere.
Updating from 2.6 — what to do first
NEW Three one-time steps. (1) Your rider profile — GroupTrack asks for it the first time it opens. (2) Update your radio, if you ride with one: 2.7a moves GroupTrack to TAK messaging, so each radio needs the GroupTrack default once. GroupTrack asks at first start — Do you have a mesh radio to use with GroupTrack? — and YES takes you to GRP Awareness to connect it and apply the default. Said NO? Do it before your first ride: GRP Awareness → connect → Select a ride and apply settings to the radio → GroupTrack default. (3) Ride files — the first time you tap one, choose GroupTrack, then Always. New to GroupTrack? The Quick Start walks you through it. Manual: First start
IMPORTANT Before every ride: send the ride invite to every riderEveryone on the ride needs the same ride. Send the ride invite to every GroupTrack rider joining you — and make sure each one opens it and imports it before the ride. The ride brings the route, the trailhead and the maps. Without it, a rider sees carts as dots on an empty map and has nothing to follow. It matters even with no radio: a rider who has imported the ride can follow the route on their own tablet, and stays on course far more easily.What it means for you: when you create a ride, send it to everyone who is coming — and ask them to open it before you meet. At the trailhead, check that every rider has it.Manual: Sending a ride

Earlier releases
DOCUMENT ID: RELNOTES-2026-08-29-B
Plan a ride
This release is about one thing: the route planner is finished. Tell it where you are
starting, how far you want to go and how fast you ride, and it brings back up to six routes for you
to compare.
How it works now
The planner asks one thing at a time. An overview explains what you will get. A second screen
sets your distance and pace, and shows the ride duration as you move the sliders — set the mileage
until the hours match the day you have.
After that each step puts a short prompt at the bottom of the screen and leaves the map clear
to work on. Pick where you will park. Drop pins on places the ride should reach, if you have any
in mind. Say whether you are looping back or finishing somewhere else. Then read back what is
about to be built, and press Continue to Compare.
Comparing the six
The routes are drawn on the map, each in its own colour, next to a table showing what each one
covers. Tap a route's name to hide or unhide its line, so you can see one at a time. Tick
the ones you want and press Save Selected / Delete Unselected — the ones you do not tick
are removed.
Build the same rides again
Every route the planner builds records the settings that produced it. Open a saved route and
press Build Routes From Recipe: it reads those settings back, shows you a summary, and
rebuilds. This is how you get back the alternatives you did not keep the first time.
The button only appears on routes the planner built — a route drawn by hand or imported from
another app has no settings to rebuild from.
Sharing a route
A shared route now carries its description with it. Export one and the summary the
planner wrote travels in the file, along with the settings that built it — so whoever you send it
to can build their own six routes from your parameters. Routes imported from Gaia or onX bring
their descriptions in the same way.
Fixes worth knowing about
Searching the same area twice. If you ran a search, then ran another in the same area
without closing the app, the second set could be worse than the first — points you asked the ride
to cover were more likely to be left out. Fixed.
Adding a trailhead now selects it. Previously you had to create one and then tap it
again.
The trailhead step opens with search ready, and a blue circle shows which trails are
close enough to start a route. Move the map until the trail you want is inside it.
Search tip: follow an area name with its two-character state. The same name exists in
many states and landing in the wrong one is not obvious — the map moves, trails draw, and
everything looks right.
What is coming next
Better trail data. The trails on your device today are selected by shape alone, which
means some paved neighbourhood roads come in as trails and some dirt roads you ride do not come in
at all. The next release fixes that, and adds trail types you can filter — so you can turn hiking
trails off, or see at a glance which parts of a route are on ground built for vehicles.
⚠ One thing to expect when it arrives: your saved routes are safe and will still draw
and navigate. But rebuilding one from its recipe may return different alternatives than it does
today, because the ground the planner can see will have changed. That is the improvement working,
not a fault.
— carried forward —
DOCUMENT ID: RELNOTES-2026-08-29
2026-09-17 — importing a state outside Utah now finishes
Imports outside Utah stopped at the last step
If you imported the trails for a state other than Utah and GroupTrack closed near the end, this
was the reason. The last step checks which trails cross private land, using a land-ownership map —
and that map only covers Utah. GroupTrack was downloading it and working through all of it for every
state, including ones it could never apply to. On most tablets that ran out of memory right at the end.
It now only does that work for Utah, where the data applies, and it reads Utah's map far more
efficiently. If an import of your state stopped before, run it again.
⚠ If the import screen won't start after an import was interrupted — you pick your state and
nothing happens — close GroupTrack completely (swipe it away from your recent apps, or use Force stop in
Android's app settings) and open it again. A fix for that is coming.
Maps are ticked for you when you import
The option to download the maps along with the trails is now switched on when the import screen
opens, and easier to read. Untick it if you only want the trails.
2026-09-15 — your location, and a map that stays where you put it
Tablets and phones without their own GPS
If your device has no GPS chip, GroupTrack could not find you at all. Your cart showed
its name but no position, and the map opened on a view of the whole country instead of where you
were. The app now also asks your network connection for a location, which is how a device without
GPS knows where it is.
And it now tells you when that is what is happening. A network location works at home
and in the car park. It does not work on the trail, because there is no network out there. If
GroupTrack is locating you that way you will see a message saying so once, with the option not to
be told again.
⚠ A device with no GPS of its own needs a mesh radio to work off-grid. The radio carries
its own GPS, so it answers both problems at once — it knows where you are and it shares that with
your group. We recommend the Seeed SenseCAP Card Tracker T1000-E.
If the app cannot find you by any means at all, it now says that too, rather than quietly
showing you an empty map.
My Cart stopped fighting the zoom
On topo maps the view jumped in and out every couple of seconds. My Cart was asking to
zoom closer than the map has detail for, the map pushed back, and round it went. My Cart now asks
for the closest zoom the map you are on actually has — so it settles and stays.
You can still pinch in past that. The picture is enlarged rather than sharper, which is the
point: your tracks and waypoints stay crisp so you can place one precisely.
Searching for a place now leaves you there
Search an area from the ride map and it used to snap back to your own cart a second or two
later. Following your cart is now switched off when a search moves the map, exactly as it is
when you drag the map with your finger. Look around as long as you like; tap MY CART when you
want to come back, and following starts again.
Searching for a track, route, trail or waypoint by name is unchanged — that opens its details
without moving the map, so you stay followed.
Smaller topo downloads
Topo maps were downloading two zoom levels the app never draws. Those levels are roughly
four times the size of the one below, each, so a topo download was several times larger than it
needed to be with nothing to show for it. They are no longer fetched. Satellite is unchanged —
it has real detail at every level it offers.
⚠ The estimate shown before a download still counts those levels, so it will read higher than
what actually arrives.
Maps failing to appear
In some situations the app could lose track of which map sources it had and fall back to
a built-in list that did not include the one you had chosen — which showed up as a blank map on
every source. It now reads your actual map settings instead of guessing.
2026-09-13 — start here
Two paths below. Open the one that applies to you.
First time installing GroupTrack
1 &middot; Grant location
GroupTrack needs your location all the time — it is how the app keeps
your position on the map and how the convoy sees where you are while you ride.
Follow the prompts.
2 &middot; Choose your home state
Let it download the trails. It takes around 25 minutes and it only happens
once. After that the trails work with no signal, which is most of where you
ride.
3 &middot; Import your track history
Do this before you start building routes. Every track you bring in adds
its trails to the trail database — so the more of your riding history you
import, the more complete your map becomes.
Put your GPX files in Downloads on your Android: save them from an email
attachment, or download them straight from your navigation app.
Then tap Import Trails on the Map Features screen from the
planning map. You will be asked to pick the files.
To select several files at once, press and hold the first file, then tap the others.
4 &middot; Ride
When the app has your location, you are ready to go.
Updating from an earlier version
Your data moves once, on the first launch
GroupTrack used to keep your trails, tracks, routes and maps in your phone's
Documents folder. It now keeps them in its own storage instead.
The first time you open this version it asks you to choose a folder. Choose
Documents and allow access. Everything moves across on its own.
Your data takes a couple of minutes. Your maps are handled separately and take
longer — a large map store can run up to 15 minutes. Leave the screen open while
it works.
If there is not enough room for your maps
Maps need space to move. If there is not enough, GroupTrack tells you, and
those maps are deleted — you will need to download them again when you
have room. Everything else still moves across.
Importing tracks has changed
GroupTrack no longer searches your Downloads folder by itself. Tap
Import Trails on the Map Features screen and you will be asked to
pick the files you want.
To select several files at once, press and hold the first file, then tap the others.
And this is worth doing with your whole track history. Every track you
import adds its trails to the trail database, so bringing in years of old tracks
fills out your map in a way nothing else does. Put the GPX files in
Downloads first — from an email attachment or straight from your
navigation app.
Why the change
Google restricts which apps may keep files in shared folders like Documents.
Rather than ask for an exception, GroupTrack now stores its own data in its own
place — which is what the rules are for.
One thing worth knowing: data kept this way is removed if you uninstall the
app. Use the share options to keep a copy of any route or track you would not
want to lose.
2026-09-12 — where GroupTrack keeps your data
A one-time move, and one tap from you
GroupTrack used to keep your trails, tracks, routes and downloaded maps
in your phone's Documents folder. It now keeps them in its own storage
instead.
The first time you open this version it will ask you to select your
Documents folder. Tap it, and everything moves across on its own — trails,
tracks, routes, waypoints, your saved colours, and your downloaded maps if
there is room for them. If you are new to GroupTrack there is nothing to
move and it simply carries on.
Your maps are the slow part. Everything else takes under a minute; a large
map store can take several. Leave the screen open while it works.
Why the change
Google restricts which apps may keep files in shared folders like
Documents. Rather than ask for an exception, GroupTrack now stores its own
data in its own place — which is what the rules are for.
One thing worth knowing: data kept this way is removed if you uninstall
the app. Use the share options to keep a copy of any route or track you would
not want to lose.
2026-09-11 — your colours stay yours
The map keys now work the way you would expect
Set a trail type to the colour, line pattern or thickness you want, and
the map draws it that way from the moment it opens — on the ride map and
the planning map both. Previously your choices only reached the map after you
opened the key panel and changed something, so a setting could appear to
revert every time you restarted the app. It was never lost; the map simply
was not being told.
Routes draw solid
Saved routes were drawn with a long dashed line that was almost
indistinguishable from a solid one, even zoomed right in. They are solid now,
like every other line you can ride, and the key panel matches. Your recorded
tracks are still dashed — that pattern is visible and it tells the two
apart.
2026-09-10 — the map answers when you tap it
Tapping things on the ride map
Tapping a trail, track or route on the ride map now opens its detail
panel. Tracks in particular were hard to hit — the line is thin and dashed,
and zoomed in there was very little to aim at. There is now a wider invisible
target along every track, so a tap near the line works. Nothing looks
different.
What the categories mean
The map key panel has a new CATEGORIES EXPLAINED button at the
foot, beside My tracks and My routes. It says in plain words what each trail
type is.
Two are worth knowing before you plan on them. Rider trails are
ground you have actually ridden, so a machine has been there — a stronger
claim than any survey. Forestry / access roads are open unless posted
otherwise, so look for a sign at the gate.
Map sources
If the app was opened while it was busy — during a state import, or the
first launch after an update — it could come up showing three map sources
instead of the full list, and ignore the ones you had chosen. Restarting was
the only cure. It now recovers on its own.
2026-09-08 — the ground you have ridden becomes trails
NEW Share a route and its narrative goes with it
Send a route to another rider and they get the whole thing — the summary, what
they will see along the way, the cautions, and the settings it was built from.
They can press BUILD FROM RECIPE and search again on their own device.
They may get different routes than you did, because the recipe is a set of
instructions rather than a copy of your answer — and their trail data is not
yours.
Opened in Gaia or onX the route still reads normally; those apps see the name,
description and points and ignore the rest.
NEW Remove a trail you added
Tap one of your own rider trails and there is now a DELETE button.
Surveyed trails do not have one.
Mostly useful when a recorder was left running on the drive to the trailhead —
highways are not in the trail data, so the whole drive comes in as new ground.
FIXED Tapping a route on the ride map
It opened a small bubble, or nothing at all. It now opens the full detail
panel, the same as the planning map.
Trails, tracks and routes also draw in proper order now — trails widest and
underneath, then tracks, then routes — so where all three share ground you can
see each of them and tap the one you meant.
⭐⭐ DO THIS FIRST — import your track history before you plan a route
If you skip this, the route planner will send you the long way around
ground you have already ridden. It cannot use a trail it does not have, and
published maps are missing a great deal of what riders actually use.
The order that gets you the best routes:
Load every state you ride in — including ones you only cross into. A
ride that leaves your loaded states has no trail data underneath it.
Import your recorded TRACKS — your saved rides from onX, Gaia or
anywhere else. ⚠ Tracks, not routes: a route is a plan, a track is where you
actually went, and only a track proves the ground is rideable.
Then build your routes.
Already built routes before importing? Rebuild them. They will come
back different, and that is the point — the planner can finally see the ground
you know.
NEW Your tracks fill in what the maps miss
Published trail data leaves a lot out. Roads and tracks that get ridden every
weekend are simply not in it, and until now that ground did not exist as far as
the app was concerned.
Now, where one of your recorded tracks crosses ground with no trail underneath
it, GroupTrack adds that stretch as a trail. It is unnamed, drawn in its own
colour, and behaves like any other trail — you can filter it, tap it, and the
route planner can use it.
Tested on one rider's collection: 88 tracks produced 1,872 new trails
covering about 2,400 miles of ground that no published source had.
NEW Import your old tracks — all of them
Export every track you have from onX, Gaia or wherever else you have
kept them, and import the lot. ⚠ Tracks, not routes. A route is a plan
somebody drew; a track is where a rider actually went. Only a track is evidence
that the ground goes through.
This is the single most useful thing you can do before using the route
planner. Every track you bring in is ground the planner can then route you
over. Without them it is working from published trails alone — and it will route
you around trails you have ridden a dozen times, with no way for you to know why.
Load your states first. A ride crossing into a state you have not
imported has no trails underneath it, so the whole stretch is treated as new
ground even where trails already exist. After that the order does not matter —
each track is checked as it arrives.
NEW Add trails from tracks, on demand
There is a new ADD TRAILS FROM TRACKS button under RESYNC TRACKS on the
import panel. It reads every track you already have and adds whatever ground is
missing. Safe to press more than once — a second run finds nothing, because the
first one already covered it.
CHANGED The trail import says what it is doing
The long stretch in the middle of a state import used to sit on
Processing for ten minutes without moving. It now shows what is being
worked on and how far through it is.
The import also has a new step of its own — Trails from tracks — which
runs after your trail data has loaded and reports how many it added.
⚠ Worth knowing
Routes you built before will come back different. With more network to
work with, the planner finds rides it could not find before. That is the
improvement working.
A trail from your ride is honest, not authoritative. It says you rode
that ground — not that it is maintained, public, or open to anyone else. Check
ownership and access the way you would anywhere else.
2026-09-04 — hide the radio panels if you do not use them
The Meshtastic column folds away
The list down the left side of the app belongs to Meshtastic, the radio
software GroupTrack is built on. If you ride with a tablet alone, none of it is
for you.
Hide Mesh at the bottom of that column folds the whole thing away.
A Mesh button then appears with Map Features and Help on the right of
either map — tap it to bring the column back. GroupTrack remembers which you
chose.
The radio menu says what it is for
The GroupTrack tab is now GroupTrack Mesh Radio Setup, and the menu
behind it is titled the same. Everything in it is radio work and nothing else,
so it is clear at a glance whether it concerns you.
Its five entries now name what they do — creating a ride's radio
configuration, sending it, importing one, applying it to your radio, and
restoring a saved one. The Map Settings section has gone; everything live in it
is reachable elsewhere.
Saved routes are named more sensibly
Saving several routes from one search used to give them all the same name.
They now carry a number — Broken Ridge Route 1, 2, and so on.
The mileage and point count have come out of the name, since tapping a route
shows the distance and riding time anyway.
Routes you saved before this keep the names they have.
2026-09-03 — tap a route and see what the ride is
One tap from the map to the ride
Tap any route you have saved and it opens with the description of the ride —
how far, how long, what you will see, and the stops in the order you reach them.
Previously that was three screens away.
The long lists start folded so the distance, the riding time and the warnings
are what you see first. Tap a heading to open one.
Two things you can do from there without leaving: Download maps for the
route's area, and Route details for the full record.
Routes built before the app started writing descriptions open the details
panel as they always did.
The import tells you the truth about itself
Classifying the trails — working out which are motorized and which sit on
private ground — is now listed as its own step when a state loads, with its own
count. Before, it ran silently at the end and a failure could look like a
finished import.
And the summary at the end of an import now waits for you. If you put the
phone down while a state loads and come back later, it is still there.
Smaller things
Only one state import runs at a time, and cancelling one actually
stops it.
Riding time shows as a range in the comparison table, not just the
faster number.
Each trail in a comparison shows its surface beside the mileage.
Tapping a trail on the ride map opens its record, as it already did on
the planning map.
Search sits where the other buttons do on both maps.
Field names read as English — Roughness rather than smoothness, Land rather
than land_status.
⚠ This update reloads your trails
The first launch after installing clears the trail data and asks you to import
your state again — about twenty minutes for a large state. A red
SYSTEM HOUSEKEEPING message appears while it prepares, and Continue turns
on by itself when it is safe.
Your maps, tracks, routes and waypoints are not affected.
2026-09-02 — choose which trails you see, and pick your own colours
Choosing what shows moved to Map Features
Yesterday's Map Keys panel did two jobs. It now does one. Which trails appear is chosen from
Map Features › Trails › SELECT — the same place you have always chosen what shows for tracks,
waypoints and routes. Everything is in one place instead of trails being the exception.
That panel has the two groups, Motorized and Non-motorized, with a tick beside each type, and a
single Include private land option. Untick a type and it goes; tap a heading and the whole
group goes. And OFF on the Trails row still hides every trail in one tap when you want the map
clear.
Map Keys is now the key — and where you set the colours
It shows what each line means. Tap the name of any type and you can change its colour, its
pattern and how thick it draws. The panel shows the line as it is now beside the line as it would be,
so you can compare before you commit. Apply, and the map changes.
What you choose is yours and it stays. The colours the app ships with are simply a starting point.
The lines tell you what you can ride
Solid lines are motorized. Dotted lines are not. That is the first thing to read on the map,
and it does not depend on telling colours apart in bright sun.
The app now also ships knowing, for every trail, whether it sits on public or private ground and
whether it is a motorized route — worked out during the import from the state's land-ownership records
and from what each source published. That is what the filter acts on.
Tap a trail and see what is actually known about it
Trails used to show a small bubble with a name. They now open the same detail card that tracks and
routes do, showing everything the sources published and nothing they did not — the surface, who
manages it, any posted restrictions, and where the record came from.
Where a trail carries a roughness rating it is written plainly: "Severe — ATV or tractor"
rather than a code. It is only recorded on a minority of trails, but where it exists it is the one
thing that tells you whether a machine will get through.
Smaller things
Search now moves the map to what you pick. Choosing a result frames it — no second step.
Search has a close button. So do Map Features, the route toolbar and the comparison table.
Route+ has an X that closes it without discarding your work. Closing and discarding are
different things and now look different.
Help offers three documents — Quick Start, Release Notes and the Full Manual — and a Cancel
if you opened it by accident.
The comparison table can be dragged out of the way.
Route planning builds on the trails you have chosen to see. If you hide a type, the planner
stops using it. What is on the map is what gets routed.
⚠ This update reloads your trails
The first launch after installing clears the trail data and asks you to import your state again.
It takes about twenty minutes for a large state. This is necessary — the new information about land
ownership and trail type is worked out during the import, and it cannot be added to data that is
already loaded.
Your maps, tracks, routes and waypoints are not affected. Only trail data reloads.
⚠ Worth knowing on first run
The app starts by showing motorized trails on public land. Hiking, biking and equestrian
trails are hidden, and so is private ground. That is deliberate for an off-road app — but if you are
looking for a trail you know exists and cannot see it, that is why. Map Features › Trails › SELECT
turns them back on.
2026-09-01 — the map key becomes a filter, and the town roads can be turned off
A new Map Keys panel, on both maps
The key that explains the colours has become something you can use. It is on the convoy map now
as well as the planning map — the convoy map never had one before. On the convoy map it opens from
the new Map Keys button, between Map Features and Help.
Inside it, the trail types are grouped into Motorized and Non-motorized, side by
side. Every type starts switched on. Unchecking a row hides that type; tapping a column heading
hides the whole group.
Public and private land
The panel has one filter at the top: Both, Public, or Private. Choosing
Public hides everything that sits on private land — which, near a town, is most of the street grid.
If you have been zooming past a mess of residential streets to find the trail you actually want,
this is the switch for that.
Choosing Private does the opposite, which is useful when a private road is how you get from one
piece of public ground to the next.
Whatever you choose is remembered and applied the next time you open the map.
The colours changed
Anything you can ride is now a shade of blue, and the shade tells you how confident the app is:
Brightest blue — an OHV route, stated as such by the people who manage it
Blue — a track
Darker blue — a forestry or access road
Faint dashed blue — the app knows a line is there and nothing more
Green, yellow, purple and brown are walking, biking and horse trails. Deep pink is a residential
road on private land. A red dashed line means the trail is recorded as unofficial or uncertain —
worth knowing before you commit to it.
More detail behind each trail
The app now keeps a great deal more of what each source publishes — surface, trail class, which
system it belongs to, which agency manages it, and any posted restrictions. None of it is on screen
yet; it is being kept so it can be shown, and used for route building, in a coming release.
Known issue
Some trails that are in the app's records are not drawing on the map. We have confirmed the trail
data itself is correct and are tracing where they are being lost on the way to the screen. If you
know a trail exists and cannot see it, that is this problem and not your data.
2026-08-31 — better trail information
Trail data now carries what the source published about each piece of ground —
its type, who manages it, and whether it sits on public or private land. It is
what makes the trail filter and the land setting work.
Much of this is groundwork you will not see directly. What you will notice is
that tapping a trail tells you more than it used to.
2026-08-30 — the app stops freezing when trail data is cleared
Clearing trail data could lock the app up on startup. It no longer does.
The rest of this release was work on how trail data is brought in and sorted —
nothing visible, but it is what the classification and filtering are built on.
2026-08-29 — build the same rides again, and a fix worth knowing about
Build six more routes from a route you kept
Open any route the planner built for you and you will find Build Routes From Recipe under
its overview. One press and it rebuilds from the same settings — the same starting point, the same
distance, the same points you asked it to cover — and shows you what it is about to do before it
runs.
The button only appears on routes the planner built. A route you drew by hand, or imported from
somewhere else, has no settings to rebuild from.
A fix: searching the same area twice
If you searched an area, then searched it again without closing the app, the second set of
rides could be worse than the first. Points you asked the ride to cover were more likely to be
left out. This is fixed — the second search now starts from the same clean slate as the first.
Also in this release
The trailhead step opens with search ready, and a blue circle shows which trails are
close enough to start a route. Move the map until the trail you want is inside it.
Adding a trailhead now selects it. Previously you had to create one and then tap it
again.
Search tip: follow an area name with its two-character state — the same name often
exists in several states, and landing in the wrong one is not obvious.
The route toolbar no longer appears over the planning screens.
Route details shows Overview rather than Narrative.
